entry: Soft fabric cushion used to support the head or body. Pillows are a form of bedding that supports the head and neck, though some are purely decorative. In contemporary Western culture they are encased in a fabric pillowcase filled with synthetic or natural stuffing. Pillows are primarily associated with sleep, while cushions are generally used for sitting or reclining. The earliest recorded use of the pillow dates to [[Mesopotamia]] around 7,000 BC, when only the wealthy used them and their number signified status. In [[Ancient Egypt]], pillows were wooden or stone headrests placed under the heads of the dead. The Romans and Greeks stuffed softer pillows with reeds, [[Feather|feathers]] and straw, but only upper-class people typically owned them.

Genus of large oceanic dolphins, with two living species, *Globicephala melas* and *G. macrorhynchus*. The long-finned and short-finned pilot whales are hard to tell apart at sea. They are among the largest oceanic dolphins, exceeded in size only by the [[Orca]]. They feed mainly on [[Squid|squid]] and stay with their birth pods throughout their lives. Short-finned pilot whales are among the few non-primate mammals in which females experience [[Menopause|menopause]]. The whales often strand on beaches; marine biologists suggest noise pollution damages their inner ear, their main navigational sonar. Both species are rated least concern.

Family of games in which a ball bounces off obstacles on a specially designed table. The early table was studded with nails called pins, and pockets scored points if the ball came to rest in them. Today pinball is most commonly an [[Arcade game|arcade]] game played on a machine with lights, bumpers and ramps. Its ancestor, bagatelle, took shape on French billiard tables during the reign of [[Louis XIV]] (1643–1715). Spring launchers, which shoot the ball up the playfield, became mainstream in 1869 and remain in use. In 1947 Gottlieb's *Humpty Dumpty* introduced player-controlled flippers, shifting the game toward skill. Pinball machines were banned in New York, Los Angeles and [[Chicago]] from the 1940s to the 1970s over perceived links to gambling and juvenile delinquency. Manufacturers active today include Stern Pinball and Jersey Jack Pinball.

Genus of coniferous trees and shrubs in the family Pinaceae. Pines bear needles in bunches, usually of two to five, and seeds in woody cones. They are widely distributed across the Northern Hemisphere, occupying large areas of [[Taiga|taiga]] (boreal forest), and also grow in Mediterranean and dry tropical habitats. Some species are fire-resistant or fire-dependent. Many pines typically reach 100–1,000 years; the Great Basin bristlecone pine (*Pinus longaeva*) is the longest-lived, and one individual in California's White Mountains, nicknamed "Methuselah," is about 4,800 years old. The tallest, a sugar pine in [[Yosemite National Park]], measures 83.45 m (273.8 ft). Pine timber is among the most widely used, and [[Pine nut|pine nuts]] are used in dishes such as pesto.

Edible seed of certain pine species. Of the 29 pine species with edible seeds, about 20 are traded locally or internationally, because their seeds are large enough to harvest. Pine nuts are not true nuts; as [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperm]] seeds, they are bare rather than enclosed in a fruit. Korean pine (*Pinus koraiensis*) is the most important species in international trade. The biggest exporters are [[China]], [[Russia]], North Korea and Pakistan. In Europe, the stone pine (*Pinus pinea*) has been cultivated for its nuts for over 5,000 years.

Tropical plant in the family Bromeliaceae, grown for its edible fruit. The pineapple, *Ananas comosus*, is the most economically significant plant in its family. It is native to [[South America]], where it was cultivated for many centuries. Its introduction to Europe in the 17th century made it a cultural icon of luxury, and since the 1820s it has been grown commercially in greenhouses and tropical plantations. Pineapples grow as small shrubs that typically mature within a year. A plant usually produces up to 200 flowers, whose berries fuse into one multiple fruit. In the wild, pineapples are pollinated mainly by [[Hummingbird|hummingbirds]]. In [[Hawaii]], where pineapples were canned industrially throughout the 20th century, importing hummingbirds was prohibited. The plant fixes [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] at night to reduce photorespiration.

Pale tint of red, named after pinks, flowering plants of the genus *Dianthus*. The term was first used as a color name in the late 17th century, and derives from the frilled edge of the flowers. Pink is generally considered a tint of red, though most pinks are slightly bluish. A combination of pink and white is associated with innocence, while pink and black suggests eroticism and seduction. Before the second half of the 20th century, pink often reflected masculinity; scholars link its feminization to the emergence of [[Barbie]] in 1959. Pink was rare in medieval fashion, but in 13th- and 14th-century religious art the Christ child was sometimes dressed in it, a color associated with the body of Christ. In [[Raphael]]'s *Madonna of the Pinks*, the child offers a pink flower to the Virgin Mary, a symbol of spiritual marriage. [[Homer]] described rosy-fingered dawn in the *Odyssey*. In the 1930s designer Elsa Schiaparelli popularized shocking pink.

English rock band formed in London in 1965. Originally one of the first British psychedelic groups, Pink Floyd became a leading progressive rock band known for extended compositions, sonic experiments and elaborate live shows. With Syd Barrett as main songwriter, they released the hit singles "Arnold Layne" and "See Emily Play" in 1967. After Barrett left in 1968, [[Roger Waters]] became the primary lyricist and devised the concepts for *The Dark Side of the Moon* (1973), *Wish You Were Here* (1975), *Animals* (1977) and *The Wall* (1979). Waters left in 1985, and David Gilmour and Nick Mason continued as Pink Floyd. The band has sold more than 250 million records and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1996.

American singer and songwriter known for a powerful vocal range and [[Acrobatics|acrobatic]] stage presence. After signing with LaFace Records in 1995, she was briefly part of the girl group Choice. Her albums *The Truth About Love* (2012), *Beautiful Trauma* (2017) and *Hurts 2B Human* (2019) all topped the US Billboard 200. She has sold more than 135 million records worldwide and has won three [[Grammy Awards]], two Brit Awards and seven [[MTV]] Video Music Awards.

Clade of semiaquatic, fin-footed carnivorous mammals, commonly called seals. Its 34 living species belong to three families: Phocidae (the earless, or true, seals), Otariidae (the eared seals, such as sea lions and fur seals) and Odobenidae, whose only living member is the [[Walrus]]. Pinnipeds belong to the order Carnivora, and their closest relatives are musteloids such as weasels, skunks and [[Red panda|red pandas]], from which they diverged about 50 million years ago. Species range from the 1 m Baikal seal to the southern elephant seal, which reaches 5 m. Most species prefer colder waters, and they come ashore to mate, give birth and molt, or to avoid predators such as [[Shark|sharks]] and [[Orca|orcas]]. A layer of blubber keeps them warm, and all species except the walrus are covered in fur. The Mediterranean and Hawaiian monk seals are endangered, and the Japanese sea lion and Caribbean monk seal became extinct in the past century.

Unit of volume or capacity in the imperial and U.S. customary systems, equal to one-eighth of a [[Gallon|gallon]]. The imperial pint, about 568 mL, is used in the United Kingdom, Ireland and other Commonwealth countries. The U.S. liquid pint is about 473 mL, and the less common dry pint about 551 mL. The imperial pint is 20.095% larger than the U.S. pint because the British redefined their system in 1824, whereas the U.S. system derives from earlier English units. Australia, South Africa and New Zealand converted to the [[Metric system|metric system]] in the 1960s and 1970s.

American social media service for discovering and sharing images, recipes and ideas on digital pinboards. Pinterest, Inc., founded by Ben Silbermann, Paul Sciarra and Evan Sharp, is headquartered in [[San Francisco]]. It grew out of Tote, an app that served as a virtual paper catalog, after Tote users were found collecting and sharing favorite items. A closed beta launched in March 2010, and an [[IPhone|iPhone]] app followed in March 2011. In 2012 the company launched business accounts. In 2017 Pinterest removed its "like" feature, converting liked posts into boards. The company reported 619 million monthly active users in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Face-on intermediate spiral galaxy in the constellation [[Ursa Major]]. Also known as Messier 101 (M101) or NGC 5457, it was discovered by Pierre Méchain in 1781, and Charles Messier verified its position for his catalog. On February 28, 2006, [[NASA]] and the [[European Space Agency]] released an image composed of 51 exposures, at the time the largest and most detailed image of a galaxy taken by the [[Hubble Space Telescope]]. The galaxy has around a trillion stars and a diameter of 252,000 light-years, compared with 87,400 light-years for the [[Milky Way]]. Its spiral arms host many bright [[H II region|H II regions]], 1,264 of which were cataloged in a 1990 study. Gravitational interaction with its companion galaxies may have produced its grand design pattern.

Most common romanization system for Standard Chinese, official in [[China]], [[Singapore]] and the [[United Nations]]. Pinyin means "spelled sounds." Each syllable is spelled with an optional initial and a final, and diacritics mark the four tones, though these are often omitted in non-Chinese texts. It was developed in the 1950s by linguists including Zhou Youguang, called the "father of pinyin," and promulgated in 1958. The International Organization for Standardization adopted it as ISO 7098 in 1982. Pinyin is used to teach Standard Chinese, which is normally written with [[Chinese characters]]. [[Taiwan]] adopted it as its official system in 2009, replacing Tongyong Pinyin.

Lightest of the [[Meson|mesons]], a subatomic particle made of a [[Quark|quark]] and an antiquark. There are three pions: π⁰, π⁺ and π⁻. Charged pions decay after a mean lifetime of 26.033 nanoseconds, mostly into muons and neutrinos. The neutral pion decays in 8.5×10⁻¹⁷ seconds, usually into gamma rays. Hideki Yukawa predicted in 1935 the mesons that carry the strong nuclear force; pions were confirmed in 1947 (charged) and 1950 (neutral). Virtual pion exchange explains the residual [[Strong interaction|strong interaction]] between nucleons.

Tubular section or hollow cylinder, usually of circular cross-section, used mainly to convey fluids, slurries and powders. A hollow pipe is far stiffer per unit weight than a solid member, so pipes are also used structurally, as in handrails and scaffolding. Pipe is usually specified by nominal diameter and a schedule that sets wall thickness, while tube is typically specified by outside diameter and wall thickness. Pipes imply rigidity and permanence, unlike flexible hoses, and are usually assembled with fittings such as elbows and tees. Uses include [[Plumbing|plumbing]], irrigation and [[Pipeline|pipelines]] carrying gas or liquid over long distances. The first known use of pipes was in [[Ancient Egypt]], where the Pyramid of Sahure, completed around the 25th century BC, included more than 380 m (1,247 ft) of copper piping. Early steel pipes were riveted, and by the early 1930s welding had replaced riveting.

Musical instrument that produces sound by driving pressurized air, or wind, through pipes. Each pipe produces one pitch, and pipes of the same tonal quality are grouped into ranks, which the player selects with controls called stops. Most organs have one or more keyboards, called manuals, and a pedalboard for the feet. The largest can have over 33,000 pipes and seven manuals. Its ancestor, the hydraulis of [[Ancient Greece]] in the 3rd century BC, used displaced water to supply wind. In 757 the Byzantine emperor Constantine V sent an organ to Pepin the Short, King of the [[Franks]], and in 812 Pepin's son [[Charlemagne]] requested one for his chapel in [[Aachen]]. By the 17th century, most sounds of the modern classical organ had been developed.

System of pipes for long-distance transport of liquids or gases, usually to a market area. Pipelines carry crude and refined [[Petroleum|petroleum]], [[Natural gas|natural gas]], hydrogen, water, sewage and other fluids. Oil pipelines are usually buried steel or plastic tubes, with pump stations along their length. Pipelines are generally the most economical way to move large quantities of oil or gas over land; in 2014, pipeline transport of crude oil cost about $5 per barrel, while rail cost about $10 to $15. In the United States, 70% of crude oil and petroleum products are shipped by pipeline. The first crude oil pipeline was built in Pennsylvania in the 1860s. Pipelines are among the safest ways to transport materials, though in war they are often military targets. [[Corrosion|Corrosion]] and leakage are the main sources of pollution from pipelines.

Robbery or criminal violence at sea by attackers from ships or boats, usually aimed at stealing cargo or taking hostages. The earliest documented piracy dates to the 14th century BC, when the [[Sea Peoples]] raided ships in the Aegean and Mediterranean. Narrow channels such as [[Gibraltar]], the [[English Channel]] and the [[Strait of Malacca]] have long offered opportunities for attack. Romanticized images of pirates owe much to *A General History of the Pyrates* (1724) and to novels such as *Treasure Island* (1883). Modern piracy is mainly armed robbery off the Somali coast, in the [[Gulf of Guinea]] and in the Strait of Malacca, often carried out from small motorboats. The International Maritime Bureau recorded 116 incidents in 2024, the lowest since 1994.

Freshwater fish of the subfamily Serrasalminae, in the order [[Characiformes]], native to South American rivers. The name comes from Old Tupi *pirãîa*, first recorded in a Portuguese–Tupi dictionary of 1585. Piranhas inhabit the Amazon basin, the [[Orinoco]], the Paraguay–Paraná and the [[São Francisco River]] systems, and most species are restricted to one river system. Estimates of the number of species range from fewer than 30 to more than 60. Most grow to between 12 and 35 cm (5–14 in) long, and the largest living species, the red-bellied piranha, reaches 50 cm (20 in). Although often portrayed as predators that feed mainly on fish, piranhas are omnivorous and also eat plant material. Many reported piranha captures are misidentifications of pacu, and piranhas are popular in the [[Aquarium|aquarium]] trade.

Small to medium-sized tree of the [[Cashew|cashew]] family, grown for its edible seeds. Pistachio trees grow up to 10 m (33 ft) tall, and male and female flowers are borne on separate trees. The seed, a culinary rather than botanical nut, sits inside a hard shell that splits open as the fruit ripens, a trait selected by humans. Trees take 7 to 10 years to reach significant production and may live up to 300 years. Pistachios are a priority allergen. In 2024 world production was 1.4 million [[Tonne|tonnes]], with the United States, Iran and Turkey accounting for 87% of the total.

Type of [[Handgun|handgun]] characterized by a barrel with an integral chamber. The word derives from the Middle French *pistolet*, meaning a small gun or knife, and entered English around 1570, when early handguns were produced in Europe. In colloquial use, "pistol" often describes any handgun, including [[Revolver|revolvers]] and derringers. The most common type today is the semi-automatic pistol. Fully automatic machine pistols are uncommon in civilian use, partly because of poor recoil control and strict laws, and they are regarded as [[Submachine gun|submachine guns]]. U.S. federal law defines a pistol as a weapon with a chamber integral to the barrel and a short stock; the definition includes derringers but excludes revolvers.

British Overseas Territory of four volcanic islands in the southern [[Pacific Ocean]]. Only Pitcairn Island is inhabited; Henderson Island makes up 86% of the territory's land, about 47 sq km (18 sq mi). The territory had 35 permanent residents in 2023, the smallest of any territory in the world. Islanders descend mainly from nine mutineers of HMS *Bounty* and Tahitian women. Polynesians settled the islands earlier and abandoned them. Pitcairn Island was sighted in 1767 by HMS *Swallow* and named after midshipman Robert Pitcairn, who first saw it. [[James Cook]] failed to find it in 1773. Widespread sexual abuse went undetected until 1999, culminating in a 2004 trial.

Second-most populous city in Pennsylvania and county seat of Allegheny County, where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers meet to form the [[Ohio River]]. The city had 302,971 residents at the 2020 census, and its metropolitan area has over 2.43 million. Known as the "Steel City" for its dominant role in U.S. steel, Pittsburgh suffered massive layoffs as heavy industry declined in the late 20th century. Since the 1990s it has focused on healthcare, education and technology, and it is home to large medical providers and 68 colleges and universities. Named in 1758 for British statesman William Pitt, the city hosted the G20 summit in 2009. Its major league teams include the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]].

Professional American football team based in Pittsburgh, competing in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Founded in 1933 as the Pittsburgh Pirates, it is the seventh-oldest NFL franchise and the oldest in the AFC. The team has been owned by the Rooney family since its founding. Before the merger it was often a losing franchise, but since then it has been among the NFL's most successful. It is tied with the [[New England Patriots]] for the most [[Super Bowl]] titles, with six, and has won eight AFC championships. It plays home games at Acrisure Stadium on Pittsburgh's North Side.
